abstract: Background: Prions are proteins that can self-template, giving rise to non-Mendelian inheritance. They are functionally diverse and have been found in all domains of life and even beyond cellular life within viruses, a distribution that suggests an ancient evolutionary origin. Testing that origin has been difficult, as prions are identified by composition, such as an enrichment of Q/N residues, and are carried by rapidly changing disordered domains that are difficult to study phylogenetically. Long terminal repeat (LTR) retroelements, mobile genetic elements that replicate through an RNA intermediate and include both retrotransposons and retroviruses, are well suited to investigate prion evolution. Prion-like domains (PrLDs) occur in their Gag proteins, while their conserved Pol proteins allow phylogenetic reconstruction independent of the domains themselves. Results: Here, we screened 2,636 proteins from mobile genetic elements in the GyDB and identified 26 PrLDs. All 26 occurred in Gag, the only one of 74 protein categories to carry them, and this association remained significant when proteins were matched for intrinsic disorder, indicating that PrLDs are not a by-product of the high disorder of Gag. Gag PrLDs were found mainly in the C-terminal half of the protein. Their composition matched that of validated yeast and archaeal prion domains in glutamine and asparagine enrichment and charge depletion, with elevated aromatic content in common with the archaeal domains and an unusually high proline content. Across a phylogeny of 258 elements built from Pol, PrLD presence was clustered rather than randomly distributed, the root was reconstructed as PrLD-positive, and losses outpaced gains by roughly eighteenfold. Conclusions: Our findings establish PrLDs as a general feature of Gag across LTR retroelements, reveal a proline-rich composition that sets them apart from characterised prion domains, and trace their presence to the ancestor of these elements. Their retention across three superfamilies despite frequent loss points to maintenance rather than repeated acquisition. By mapping a compositionally defined domain onto a phylogeny built from conserved proteins, this work allows the gain and loss of prion-like sequence to be reconstructed and provides 26 candidates for experimental testing.
